turn_text: David Perdue, welcome back. Well, thanks, Wes. It's great to be here live, man. This is good.

It is. It's great to have you in studio. We do a lot over the phone, so it's always great when you're here and you're having some time to stop by and see us. You've been busy, though, this week. I guess visit to the Kia plant, and those guys are sharp, aren't they?

Oh, man, I'm telling you, you know, last week I was all over South Georgia meeting with farmers and all that, and yesterday I was at Kia early this week, and They are so impressive. I'm telling you, they're about to celebrate their 10th year. They're about to celebrate or put out their third or the three millionth car. You can believe that in 10 years. And they export from here as well. I mean, what they're doing down there is so impressive. They train in a way that I've not seen anybody do before. And it's a great marriage between the Korean manufacturing mindset, and the American worker, and an amazing marriage of that. I'm telling you, they're one of the best.
It certainly meant a lot to this community, and not only the jobs and what it's done for us economically, I don't know where we'd be right now without it.

Well, you know, we had the textile industry in that part of the world kind of came and went in the 20th century, and so you had these workers and descendants of workers in the area, and we always kept saying if someone would come in there, and sure enough, under Governor Perdue, They attracted Kia to come in and Kia saw what they had there. And it wasn't just the workers in their plan. It's all the vendors and the support companies that came with it. I mean, they're still developing capabilities out there. You know, the front end of the car is done by a vendor that's right there on site and works very well. Everything is just in time. They don't have any excess inventory. And as an old manufacturing guy, I can tell you, you can eat on the floor of that place. It's incredible. And yet with all the robotics and everything else, all the technology, they still employ a lot of people. When they assemble the car, it comes down to the human touch, as they say. When the interior goes in, the steering wheel goes on, the tires get put on, it's the human touch that really makes it work. A bit of a rush when you see it all happen. I'm a gear head anyway, Wes. And so you see the engine going in there and the cars coming off, these SUVs are just, they're great. But the thing that impressed me most was people. I mean, everybody we saw, there was a shift change when we were there. So we actually saw the better parts of two shifts. Everybody had smiles on their face. They were glad to be at work. It wasn't an onerous, assembling line type mentality. And one thing I learned from the careers, I lived in Pusan for a while in South Korea briefly. And they rotate jobs so that people don't get bored doing the same thing all day long, you know? And I thought that was really unique
in that factory. takes away from the monotony of it. You also visited Fort Benning this week. Oh, we did. We had a great visit

with General Brito and his staff over there this week. Every time I come to Benning, I just get chill bumps thinking about the men and women who have dedicated their career. You know, I see these troops when they're deployed in Afghanistan. We're about to have some people go to Africa. We've got people all over the world coming through Benning. I mean, in all levels, I mean, they bring officers back into Benning to get trained up lieutenant kernels and kernels for major commands and then of course there are all the 17 year old recruits going through basic here and then the jump school we drove by that today and I committed that you know when we honor the golden nights next time I'm gonna be down here and jump out of a plane with them so I am so impressed that Georgia over the years since World War II has had Fort Benning here is a huge asset but it's it's more than just land and and all that it's people in the community here does such a great job of supporting this base.

And we got you here just before you head to China and obviously China is top of mind for a lot of us right now and a big impact on the economy in general. So what you got in store for the folks in China when you get there.

Well, I hope it does a reality, but I lived in Singapore and Hong Kong during my career and worked in China a good bit over the last 30 years. Steve Baines, the Senator from Montana and I are going over. This is a repeat trip we were over there last year. We've met with them earlier this year in Washington. This is an ongoing dialogue. We hope to add weight behind what the President and the Trade Representatives are doing in their negotiation. We're not directly part of that negotiation, of course, but we do add weight behind the fact that America is serious and that we need China to begin to comply. And there are some very simple things that we want. Look, nobody likes tariffs West, but the President, who can fault him for trying to develop a level playing field? I mean, around the world. I've watched as the U.S. trade rules in our Navy have secured trade around the world, and we've helped develop the third world. We really have. Global poverty has been reduced over the last 60 years by some 60 percent, largely because of our efforts to develop the rest of the world. Now it's time for us to have equal access. So what President Trump is trying to do is tell our allies and China, look, if you can sell stuff here, we won't be able to sell stuff there. It's just that simple. And I believe we'll win out in the long term, but we're also trying to do some other things. We want them to stop stealing our technology. We want them to stop the force transfer of technology and our joint ventures over there. We want them to comply with the WTO and we want them to stop the cyber war and give us equal access. And we've got major agreements on equal access, but we're trying to get these other areas tied down there. And that's what the conversation is all about.
